Can you schedule these with preemptive priority? P1 arrives at 0 and needs 1 ms with priority 5; P2 arrives at 0 and needs 3 ms with priority 2; P3 arrives at 2 and needs 8 ms with priority 3; P4 arrives at 2 and needs 7 ms with priority 4. (Lower number = higher priority.)

**Rule.** Preemptive priority (lower number = higher priority): the highest-priority ready process runs, and a newcomer preempts it only if its priority is strictly higher.

**Decisions**
- t = 0: CPU is free; P2 has the highest priority among the ready processes (priority 2).
- t = 2: P3, P4 arrived, but no ready process has a higher priority than running P2 (priority 2), so P2 continues.
- t = 3: CPU is free; P3 has the highest priority among the ready processes (priority 3).
- t = 11: CPU is free; P4 has the highest priority among the ready processes (priority 4).
- t = 18: CPU is free; P1 has the highest priority among the ready processes (priority 5).

**Gantt chart:** [0–3] P2 → [3–11] P3 → [11–18] P4 → [18–19] P1

**Table** (TAT = CT − AT, WT = TAT − BT)
| Process | AT | BT | CT | TAT | WT |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| P1 | 0 | 1 | 19 | 19 | 18 |
| P2 | 0 | 3 | 3 | 3 | 0 |
| P3 | 2 | 8 | 11 | 9 | 1 |
| P4 | 2 | 7 | 18 | 16 | 9 |

Average TAT = (19 + 3 + 9 + 16) / 4 = 11.75

What do our notes say about Processes with I/O bursts?

For CPU 4, I/O 3, CPU 3: after the first CPU burst the process leaves the ready queue for 3 units (I/O runs in parallel with the CPU) and returns to the ready queue when the I/O ends. Completion time is the end of the last CPU burst. The 2026-27 key uses WT = TAT − (all CPU bursts) − (I/O burst). When a paper says "each process spends 25% of its time on I/O", the 2025-26 key treated the I/O as happening first and counted it as waiting (WT = TAT − CPU). State the convention you use in the exam.

Multiprocessor scheduling – worked examples: what should I know for the exam?

AMP example: core 0 is the master (runs OS code, scheduling and all I/O, FCFS I/O queue); cores 1–3 run user CPU bursts, assigned FCFS. Each process has a CPU burst then an I/O burst on the master: P1 (AT 0, CPU 4, I/O 2), P2 (1, 3, 3), P3 (2, 2, 1), P4 (3, 5, 2). Is SJF preemptive?

SJF can be either. Non-preemptive SJF picks the shortest burst when the CPU becomes free and lets it finish. The preemptive version is SRTF (OSTEP calls it STCF): a newly arrived process with a strictly shorter remaining time takes the CPU at once.

Here's my understanding of semaphores: so basically signal() (v) increases s; if processes are waiting, one of them can now proceed. blocking version: a negative value −k means k processes are waiting. busy-waiting version (module 4 p/v): s stays at 0 and the waiting processes spin. wait() (p) decreases s; a process that cannot get it waits (blocking version: blocks when s becomes negative; module 4 version: loops while s ≤ 0).

What you got right:
- wait() (P) decreases S; a process that cannot get it waits (blocking version: blocks when S becomes negative; Module 4 version: loops while S ≤ 0).
- signal() (V) increases S; if processes are waiting, one of them can now proceed.
- Blocking version: a negative value −k means k processes are waiting. Busy-waiting version (Module 4 P/V): S stays at 0 and the waiting processes spin.

What's missing:
- A binary semaphore (initial 1) works as a mutex: wait before, signal after the critical section.
- Order of waits matters: holding mutex while waiting on another semaphore can deadlock.

Test me on scheduling basics

Here's one:

In a non-preemptive algorithm, a more urgent process arrives while another is running. What happens?
A) It immediately takes the CPU
B) It is discarded
C) It waits until the running process finishes its burst
D) Both share the CPU
B

Not quite. It waits in the ready queue. The answer is C) It waits until the running process finishes its burst. Right: non-preemptive means nobody is interrupted.

Next one:

A process arrives at t=2, first runs at t=5 and finishes at t=9. Its burst time is 4. What is its turnaround time?
A) 9
B) 7
C) 3
D) 4
D?

Not quite. 4 is the burst time (time actually running), not the total time in the system. The answer is B) 7. Right: TAT = CT − AT = 9 − 2 = 7.

Explain Round Robin like I'm new to it

Kids sharing **one swing**: each gets 2 minutes, then goes to the back of the line, even if they wanted more. Nobody waits forever, and everyone gets a turn quickly.

**The rule.** Keep a FIFO **ready queue**. Take the process at the **front** and run it for at most one **time quantum** q.
- If it finishes within q, it leaves, and the next process starts immediately (no idle remainder).
- If not, the timer interrupts it and it goes to the **back** of the queue.

**Queue order convention (important).** If a process arrives at exactly the moment another one's quantum ends, this course puts the **new arrival in the queue first**, then the preempted process. Always track the queue on paper: write it down after every slice.

**Choosing q.** A huge q makes RR behave like FCFS. A tiny q causes too many context switches. RR usually has worse average turnaround than SJF but much better **response time**, so it suits interactive systems.

Explain Scheduling basics

A college canteen has **one billing counter** and a line of students. Only one student can be served at a time, so someone has to decide who goes next. The counter is the **CPU**, the students are **processes**, and the person deciding the order is the **scheduler**.

**Why scheduling exists.** A computer runs many processes, but one CPU core can execute only one of them at any moment. Processes that are ready to run wait in the **ready queue**. The **CPU scheduler** picks which one runs next.

**The numbers in every problem**

| Term | Meaning | How to get it |
|---|---|---|
| Arrival time (AT) | When the process enters the ready queue | Given |
| Burst time (BT) | How much CPU time it needs | Given |
| Completion time (CT) | When it finishes for good | End of its **last** block in the Gantt chart |
| Turnaround time (TAT) | Total time from arrival to completion | **TAT = CT − AT** |
| Waiting time (WT) | Time spent ready but not running | **WT = TAT − BT** |
| Response time (RT) | Wait before it runs for the first time | **RT = first start − AT** |

**Gantt chart.** A timeline showing which process holds the CPU in each interval. If no process has arrived yet, the CPU is **idle**.

**Preemptive vs non-preemptive.** Non-preemptive: once a process starts, it keeps the CPU until its burst is done. Preemptive: the OS can take the CPU away (for example when a better process arrives or a time slice ends).
Can you explain it another way?

Think of a single **printer** shared by a class. Each person arrives at some time (AT) with a print job that takes a fixed time (BT). The time you finally walk away with your pages is CT. From the moment you arrived until you left is your turnaround (TAT = CT − AT). Part of that time the printer was actually printing your pages (BT); the rest you were just standing in line, which is your waiting time (WT = TAT − BT).

**Check yourself:** you arrive at 2, leave at 9 and printing took 4. What is your waiting time?

What do our notes say about Extra slides: multi-level feedback queue?

MLFQ learns from the past to predict the future: it aims to optimise turnaround (run short jobs first) and minimise response time without knowing job lengths in advance. Rules: Rule 1: if Priority(A) > Priority(B), A runs. Rule 2: if Priority(A) = Priority(B), A and B run in Round Robin. Rule 3: a new job is placed at the highest priority. What is Scheduling basics?

**Canteen billing counter.** One cashier (the CPU) and a line of students (processes). You join the line at 12:02 (arrival), billing takes 3 minutes (burst), you leave at 12:10 (completion). You spent 8 minutes there (turnaround) but only 3 being served, so you waited 5.

**Why scheduling exists.** A computer runs many processes, but one CPU core can execute only one of them at any moment. Processes that are ready to run wait in the **ready queue**. The **CPU scheduler** picks which one runs next.

**The numbers in every problem**

| Term | Meaning | How to get it |
|---|---|---|
| Arrival time (AT) | When the process enters the ready queue | Given |
| Burst time (BT) | How much CPU time it needs | Given |
| Completion time (CT) | When it finishes for good | End of its **last** block in the Gantt chart |
| Turnaround time (TAT) | Total time from arrival to completion | **TAT = CT − AT** |
| Waiting time (WT) | Time spent ready but not running | **WT = TAT − BT** |
| Response time (RT) | Wait before it runs for the first time | **RT = first start − AT** |

**Gantt chart.** A timeline showing which process holds the CPU in each interval. If no process has arrived yet, the CPU is **idle**.

**Preemptive vs non-preemptive.** Non-preemptive: once a process starts, it keeps the CPU until its burst is done. Preemptive: the OS can take the CPU away (for example when a better process arrives or a time slice ends).

Explain first come first serve

A **railway ticket counter**: whoever reaches the line first is served first, and nobody can cut in.

**The rule.** Run processes in the order they **arrive**. FCFS is **non-preemptive**: a process keeps the CPU until its burst is finished. If two processes arrive at the same time, the one listed first goes first.

**How to solve an FCFS problem**
1. Sort the processes by arrival time.
2. Each process starts at the later of: its arrival time, or the moment the previous one finished.
3. If the CPU finishes before the next process arrives, the CPU is **idle** until it arrives.
4. Then CT, TAT = CT − AT, WT = TAT − BT.

**The convoy effect.** If a long process arrives first, every short process behind it waits for the whole long burst. Example: bursts 8, 2, 1 arriving at 0, 1, 2 give waiting times 0, 7 and 8 (average 5). If the short jobs could go first, the average would drop a lot. FCFS is simple and fair by arrival order, but its average waiting time can be poor.

round robin in simple words please

**In your laptop.** Time slices of a few milliseconds let a music player, a browser and a download all make progress, which is why the computer feels responsive.

**The rule.** Keep a FIFO **ready queue**. Take the process at the **front** and run it for at most one **time quantum** q.
- If it finishes within q, it leaves, and the next process starts immediately (no idle remainder).
- If not, the timer interrupts it and it goes to the **back** of the queue.

**Queue order convention (important).** If a process arrives at exactly the moment another one's quantum ends, this course puts the **new arrival in the queue first**, then the preempted process. Always track the queue on paper: write it down after every slice.

**Choosing q.** A huge q makes RR behave like FCFS. A tiny q causes too many context switches. RR usually has worse average turnaround than SJF but much better **response time**, so it suits interactive systems.

Summarise Comparison of preemptive algorithms for me

SRTF: always runs the process with the shortest remaining burst; a newly arrived process with a shorter remaining time preempts immediately; minimum average waiting and turnaround time; frequent context switches; long processes may starve. Preemptive priority: runs the highest-priority process; a newly arrived higher-priority process preempts immediately; low-priority processes may starve. Round Robin: each process gets a fixed time quantum, then is preempted and moved to the end of the ready queue; no starvation; fair sharing; performance depends on the quantum; many context switches; a new process joins the ready queue and waits its turn. MLFQ: several queues with different priorities and quanta; the highest-priority queue is served first; processes move between queues based on CPU usage; very low starvation (aging and promotion); hard to implement and tune; used in modern general-purpose OSs.

What do our notes say about Interrupt disabling and locks?

Solution 1, interrupt disable: a process disables all hardware interrupts before entering its critical section and enables them on exit, so nothing else can run meanwhile. Not suitable for multiprocessors: disabling interrupts on one CPU does not stop the others. Solution 2, locks: a lock lets only one process access a shared resource at a time; a process must acquire the lock first, and if another process holds it the requester is blocked until it is released. Software-based locks use flags, turn variables or tickets: Peterson's algorithm (two processes), Dekker's algorithm (more complex, two processes) and the Bakery algorithm (more than two processes, token based). Hardware-based locks use atomic instructions.

Summarise Extra slides: multiprocessor scheduling for me

Adding CPUs does not make one single-threaded application faster; it must be rewritten with threads. Caches make memory look fast but bring cache coherence problems (CPU 1 may read a stale copy after CPU 0 updates a value); bus snooping lets caches invalidate or update copies. Shared data across CPUs still needs locks (e.g. a list pop must be protected by a mutex). Cache affinity: keep a process on the same CPU where its state is cached. Single-queue multiprocessor scheduling (SQMS) puts all jobs in one shared queue: simple, but needs locking (poor scalability) and jobs bounce between CPUs (poor affinity) unless the scheduler preserves affinity for most jobs and migrates only some. Multi-queue scheduling (MQMS) gives each CPU its own queue: scalable and good affinity, but load imbalance (a CPU may sit idle or one job may get twice the CPU of others), fixed by migration and work stealing (a queue low on jobs peeks at fuller queues and steals jobs; too much peeking costs overhead). Linux schedulers: the O(1) scheduler (priority-based, multiple queues, interactivity focus) and the Completely Fair Scheduler (deterministic proportional share).

Summarise Priority scheduling for me

A priority is associated with each process and the CPU goes to the highest-priority process; equal priorities are served FCFS. SJF is a priority algorithm where priority is the inverse of the predicted next CPU burst. Priority scheduling can be preemptive (a newly arrived process with higher priority than the running one preempts it) or non-preemptive (the new process is simply put at the head of the ready queue). The notes show both conventions, smallest integer = highest priority and largest integer = highest priority; the worked examples use smallest integer = highest priority unless the question says otherwise. Problem: starvation of low-priority processes. Solution: aging, increasing the priority of a process as time passes.

What do our notes say about Test-and-Set with bounded waiting?

Shared waiting[n] and lock. Entry: waiting[i] = true; key = true; while (waiting[i] && key) key = TestAndSet(&lock); waiting[i] = false. Exit: look for the next waiting process j in circular order; if none, set lock = false, otherwise set waiting[j] = false. In the 2025-26 C2 trace, the first process whose TestAndSet sees lock = false enters; on exit it hands the critical section directly to the next waiting process in order, which gives bounded waiting.

What do our notes say about Process concept?

A process is a program in execution; its execution progresses sequentially. Its parts: the program code (text section); the current activity (program counter, processor registers); the stack (temporary data: function parameters, return addresses, local variables); the data section (global variables); the heap (memory allocated at run time). A program is a passive entity stored on disk (an executable file); a process is active, lives in memory and executes instructions. A program becomes a process when the executable is loaded into memory, and one program can become several processes.

What do our notes say about Race condition?

A race condition is a situation where two or more processes or threads access shared data concurrently, at least one modifies it, and the result depends on the order in which their operations run (who reaches certain operations first: hence "race"). Example: counter = 5 and two processes each do counter++ (read, increment a local copy, write). If A reads 5, B reads 5, both compute 6 and both write 6, the final value is 6 (wrong); if A finishes before B starts it is 7 (right). At machine level counter++ is register1 = counter; register1 = register1 + 1; counter = register1, and counter-- is the same with register2. The interleaving S0 producer register1 = counter (5), S1 register1 + 1 (6), S2 consumer register2 = counter (5), S3 register2 − 1 (4), S4 producer counter = register1 (6), S5 consumer counter = register2 (4) leaves counter = 4 instead of 5. Another example: two processes creating children at the same time could both read next_available_pid and assign the same pid to two processes.

What do our notes say about Multiprocessor scheduling – concepts?

With more than one CPU, scheduling must decide which CPU handles which task and balance the load. With identical (homogeneous) processors any processor can run any process. Processor affinity: a process prefers the processor it last ran on, because its data is in that cache; soft affinity (the OS tries but does not guarantee) vs hard affinity (restricted to a set of CPUs, e.g. sched_setaffinity() in Linux). Load balancing avoids overloaded and idle processors: push migration (a busy processor pushes tasks to less busy ones) and pull migration (an idle processor pulls tasks). Multicore processors: memory stall (waiting for data not in cache, up to 50% of the time) is hidden by hardware multithreading, coarse-grained (switch thread on a long-latency event) or fine-grained (switch every cycle). Virtualisation can distort time slices of guest OSs. Approaches: asymmetric multiprocessing (AMP), a master–slave approach where one master processor makes the scheduling decisions and does I/O while the others run only user code (simple; if a slave fails the rest keeps working, but the master is a bottleneck and a single point of failure); symmetric multiprocessing (SMP), where each processor schedules itself, with either a common ready queue or private per-CPU ready queues.

What is first come first serve?

**Bank token system.** You take token 42; tokens are served strictly in order. A person with a 1-minute job behind someone opening a new account (20 minutes) still waits the full 20 minutes: that is the convoy effect.

**The rule.** Run processes in the order they **arrive**. FCFS is **non-preemptive**: a process keeps the CPU until its burst is finished. If two processes arrive at the same time, the one listed first goes first.

**How to solve an FCFS problem**
1. Sort the processes by arrival time.
2. Each process starts at the later of: its arrival time, or the moment the previous one finished.
3. If the CPU finishes before the next process arrives, the CPU is **idle** until it arrives.
4. Then CT, TAT = CT − AT, WT = TAT − BT.

**The convoy effect.** If a long process arrives first, every short process behind it waits for the whole long burst. Example: bursts 8, 2, 1 arriving at 0, 1, 2 give waiting times 0, 7 and 8 (average 5). If the short jobs could go first, the average would drop a lot. FCFS is simple and fair by arrival order, but its average waiting time can be poor.

What do our notes say about CPU scheduling and the CPU–I/O burst cycle?

CPU scheduling is the basis of a multiprogrammed OS: by switching the CPU among processes the OS makes the computer more productive. The objective of multiprogramming is to have some process running all the time, to maximise CPU utilisation. A process runs until it must wait, typically for an I/O request to complete; several processes are kept in memory (ready queue, waiting queue), and when one has to wait the OS takes the CPU away and gives it to another. Process execution is a cycle of CPU execution and I/O wait: processes alternate between a CPU burst and an I/O burst, ending with a final CPU burst.

race conditions and the critical section in simple words please

**Shared bank account.** You and your parent withdraw ₹500 at two ATMs at the same instant from a balance of ₹1000. Without locking, both read ₹1000 and both write ₹500, so the bank loses ₹500.

**Race condition.** When several processes or threads access **shared data** at the same time, and the result depends on the exact order in which they run, you have a race condition.

**Why count++ is not safe.** In machine code it is three steps: **load** count into a register, **add** 1, **store** it back. If two threads interleave these steps, one update can be lost.

**Critical section.** The part of the code that touches shared data. A correct solution must guarantee:
1. **Mutual exclusion:** at most one process is in its critical section at a time.
2. **Progress:** if nobody is inside, a process that wants to enter cannot be blocked forever by processes that don't want to enter.
3. **Bounded waiting:** after a process asks to enter, there is a limit on how many times others can enter before it.

**Solutions.** Peterson's algorithm (two processes, using `flag[]` and `turn`), hardware atomic instructions (test_and_set, compare_and_swap), mutex locks and semaphores.

Explain Theory slides: condition variables

Locks give mutual exclusion; another common need is waiting and signalling (thread T1 continues only after T2 has finished a task). Busy-waiting on a variable works but wastes CPU, so condition variables are used: a CV is a queue a thread puts itself in while waiting for a condition; another thread that makes the condition true signals the CV (signal wakes one thread, broadcast wakes all). Example: a parent waiting for its child checks a done flag in a while loop before waiting (the child may already have finished, and some implementations wake threads spuriously). The lock must be held when calling wait and signal, otherwise a wakeup can be missed (the parent sees done = 0, is interrupted, the child sets done and signals with nobody waiting, then the parent sleeps forever); wait releases the lock before sleeping. Producer/consumer with two CVs: e.g. in a multithreaded web server one thread puts requests in a bounded shared queue and worker threads take them out.

Explain SJF – Shortest Job First

SJF associates with each process the length of its next CPU burst; when the CPU is available it goes to the process with the smallest next CPU burst. If two processes have the same next burst, FCFS breaks the tie. SJF can be non-preemptive (SJN) or preemptive (SRTF). A better name is shortest-next-CPU-burst. SJF is optimal (minimum average waiting time) but the real difficulty is knowing the length of the next CPU request, so it cannot be implemented exactly at the short-term level; it is approximated by predicting the next burst from previous ones. Example 1 (non-preemptive, all at 0): P1 6, P2 8, P3 7, P4 3. Gantt P4 0–3, P1 3–9, P3 9–16, P2 16–24. WT P1 3, P2 16, P3 9, P4 0; average 7 ms (FCFS would give 10.25 ms). Example 5 (all at 0): P1 10, P2 5, P3 8: Gantt P2 0–5, P1 5–13, P3 13–23; average TAT 13.67, average WT 6. Example 6 (different arrivals): P1 (0, 10), P2 (1, 3), P3 (2, 6), P4 (3, 4), P5 (4, 2).

Can you teach me shortest job first from scratch?

**Photocopy shop.** The shopkeeper finishes the current job, then takes the customer with the fewest pages among those already in the shop. A 1-page customer walking in mid-job must wait for that job to end.

**The rule.** Whenever the CPU becomes free, choose the process with the **shortest burst time among those that have already arrived**. SJF here is **non-preemptive**: once a process starts, it finishes. Ties are broken by arrival order.

**Two traps**
- A process that has **not arrived yet** cannot be chosen, even if it is shorter.
- A short job that arrives while another is running does **not** interrupt it (that would be SRTF).

**Why it is useful.** When all processes are available together, SJF gives the **minimum average waiting time** of any non-preemptive order: putting a short job before a long one saves the short job more waiting than it costs the long one.

**Its weaknesses.** The OS does not know the next burst length in advance; it estimates it from past bursts (exponential averaging). Long jobs can **starve** if short jobs keep arriving.

Deadlocks in concurrent programs: what should I know for the exam?

Deadlock bug, classic form: Thread 1 holds lock L1 and waits for L2 while Thread 2 holds L2 and waits for L1. It occurs only if the executions overlap and a context switch happens after a thread has acquired just one lock. It appears as a cycle in the dependency graph, and all four conditions (mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait) must hold. Preventing circular wait: acquire locks in a fixed total (or partial) order, e.g. both threads take L1 before L2, or order locks by the address of the lock variable. Preventing hold-and-wait: acquire all locks at once, e.g. by first taking a master lock (reduces concurrency). Avoidance: if the OS knew which locks each process needs it could schedule them so deadlock cannot occur (the Banker's algorithm is popular but assumes knowledge rarely available in real life). Detect and recover: reboot or kill deadlocked processes.

What do our notes say about How the OS runs a process and switches?

The OS creates a process by allocating memory and building its memory image (code and data loaded from the executable, a stack and a heap), opening the standard files (stdin, stdout, stderr) and initialising the registers so the program counter points at the first instruction; then it gets out of the way and the process runs directly on the CPU. A process consists of a PID, its memory image, its CPU context (PC, registers, stack pointer) and its open file descriptors. The OS timeshares the CPU: the policy decides which process to run, the mechanism does the context switch. System calls use a trap instruction: the CPU moves to kernel mode, switches to the kernel stack, saves the user context, and jumps to the handler found in the Interrupt Descriptor Table (IDT, set up at boot). Traps also happen on program faults and device interrupts. return-from-trap restores the context and returns to user mode. Before returning, the OS may switch to another process: when the process exited or was terminated, made a blocking call, or has run too long.

Peterson's solution: what should I know for the exam?

A two-process mutual-exclusion algorithm for P0 and P1 using two shared variables: flag[2] ("do I want to enter?", the interest) and turn ("if both want to enter, whom should I allow?", the tie-breaker). Idea: declare your interest, give priority to the other process, and wait only if the other process is interested and currently has priority. Code for Pi (j is the other process): while (true) { flag[i] = true; turn = j; while (flag[j] && turn == j); /* critical section */ flag[i] = false; /* remainder section */ }. So P0 sets flag[0] = true; turn = 1; and waits while (flag[1] && turn == 1); P1 sets flag[1] = true; turn = 0; and waits while (flag[0] && turn == 0). Cases: if only P0 wants to enter, flag[1] is false, so false && true = false and P0 enters at once (same for P1 alone). If both want to enter, both set their flags and both write turn; the last write wins. If P1 writes last (turn = 0), P0 checks flag[1] && turn == 1, which is true && false, so P0 enters; P1 checks flag[0] && turn == 0, which is true, so P1 waits until P0 sets flag[0] = false on exit.

FCFS – First Come First Serve: what should I know for the exam?

The simplest algorithm: the process that requests the CPU first is allocated it first, implemented with a FIFO queue. New processes (their PCBs) are added at the tail; when the CPU is free it goes to the process at the head, which is removed from the queue. FCFS is non-preemptive. Its average waiting time is often high and it is not suitable for time-sharing systems (convoy effect: short processes wait behind a long one).

What do our notes say about When scheduling decisions happen; preemptive vs non-preemptive?

CPU scheduling decisions may take place when a process (1) switches from running to waiting (e.g. an I/O request), (2) switches from running to ready (e.g. an interrupt), (3) switches from waiting to ready (e.g. I/O completes), (4) terminates. For 1 and 4 there is no choice: a new process must be selected. For 2 and 3 there is a choice. The scheduler runs whenever a process is created, terminates, requests I/O and blocks, an I/O completes, or a timer interrupt occurs (preemptive scheduling). How it works: processes waiting for the CPU sit in the ready queue; the scheduler picks one using an algorithm; the dispatcher assigns it to the CPU; the process then completes, requests I/O (moves to waiting), or is preempted back to the ready queue. Non-preemptive (cooperative) scheduling: decisions only in cases 1 and 4; the running process keeps the CPU until it finishes or blocks; simpler; suits batch systems; example FCFS. Preemptive scheduling: the CPU can be taken away from a running process; better responsiveness; suits interactive systems; example Round Robin.

What's the difference between starvation and deadlock?

In deadlock a set of processes all wait for each other, so none of them can ever proceed. In starvation the system keeps running, but one process is passed over again and again (e.g. a low-priority process when high-priority ones keep arriving). Aging fixes starvation; deadlock needs prevention, avoidance or detection.

What do our notes say about Independent and cooperating processes?

Processes executing concurrently are either independent (cannot affect or be affected by other processes) or cooperating (can affect or be affected by others). Any process that shares data with other processes is a cooperating process. Reasons to cooperate: information sharing, computation speed-up, modularity, convenience. Example: in a bank ATM one process reads the card and PIN, another checks the account balance and a third dispenses cash; they must communicate and coordinate. Cooperating processes need an inter-process communication (IPC) mechanism.

What do our notes say about Scheduling criteria and formulas?

CPU utilisation = CPU busy time / total time × 100 (maximise). Throughput = number of completed processes / total time (maximise). Turnaround time TAT = completion time − arrival time (minimise). Waiting time WT = time spent waiting in the ready queue = TAT − CPU burst time (minimise). Response time RT = time of first CPU allocation − arrival time (minimise). Context switches: the number of times the CPU switches between processes; pure overhead (minimise). Fairness: each process gets an equitable share (maximise). The notes also state: TAT = waiting time + CPU burst time + I/O burst time (or TAT = WT + CPU burst when there is no I/O). In non-preemptive scheduling response time = waiting time, because a process starts only once. In preemptive scheduling response time ≤ waiting time.

Multilevel queue scheduling – MLQ: what should I know for the exam?

MLQ divides the ready queue into several queues arranged in a hierarchy, e.g. system processes, interactive processes and batch processes. Each queue has its own priority level and its own scheduling algorithm (e.g. queue 1 and 2 Round Robin, queue 3 FCFS). A process is assigned permanently to one queue, based on priority, resources or process type. Scheduling among the queues: (1) fixed-priority preemptive scheduling, where each queue has absolute priority over lower queues (no batch process runs unless queues 1 and 2 are empty, and a running batch process is preempted when a system or interactive process arrives); or (2) time slicing, where each queue gets a share of CPU time (e.g. 50%, 30%, 20%). Example: P1 in Queue 1 (RR, q = 2, AT 0, BT 5), P2 in Queue 2 (FCFS, AT 1, BT 4), P3 in Queue 3 (SJF, AT 2, BT 3). Queue 1 is served first: P1 0–2, 2–4, 4–5; then P2 5–9 (FCFS, runs fully); then P3 9–12. Advantages: organised separation of process types, predictable, good response for interactive/system processes, ensures critical processes are not delayed.

Explain Round Robin

Kids sharing **one swing**: each gets 2 minutes, then goes to the back of the line, even if they wanted more. Nobody waits forever, and everyone gets a turn quickly.

**The rule.** Keep a FIFO **ready queue**. Take the process at the **front** and run it for at most one **time quantum** q.
- If it finishes within q, it leaves, and the next process starts immediately (no idle remainder).
- If not, the timer interrupts it and it goes to the **back** of the queue.

**Queue order convention (important).** If a process arrives at exactly the moment another one's quantum ends, this course puts the **new arrival in the queue first**, then the preempted process. Always track the queue on paper: write it down after every slice.

**Choosing q.** A huge q makes RR behave like FCFS. A tiny q causes too many context switches. RR usually has worse average turnaround than SJF but much better **response time**, so it suits interactive systems.

What is Priority scheduling?

**Hospital emergency.** An accident victim is treated before someone with a cold, even if the cold patient came first. If the emergency room is non-preemptive, a doctor already treating a patient finishes first.

**The rule.** Each process has a priority number. The CPU goes to the **arrived** process with the **highest priority**. In this course a **lower number means higher priority** (priority 1 beats priority 3). Some books use the opposite, so always check the question. Equal priorities are broken by arrival order.

**Two versions**
- **Non-preemptive:** a newly arrived urgent process waits until the running one finishes.
- **Preemptive:** a newly arrived process interrupts the running one if its priority is **strictly higher**.

**Starvation and aging.** A low-priority process may wait forever if higher-priority work keeps arriving. **Aging** fixes this by slowly raising the priority of processes that have been waiting a long time.

**Connections.** SJF is priority scheduling where priority = burst length; FCFS is priority scheduling where priority = arrival time.

Summarise Synchronization hardware: atomic instructions and spinlocks for me

Peterson and Bakery show that mutual exclusion is possible with shared variables, but real systems need low-level operations supported by the processor. An atomic instruction is indivisible: read–modify–write happens as one step, and once it starts nothing else (another process, an interrupt) can interfere. A spinlock uses busy waiting: the process keeps checking the lock variable until it becomes free; it is usually built from Test-and-Set or Compare-and-Swap. Instructions: Test-and-Set (tests a lock variable and sets it if free), Compare-and-Swap (compares a variable with an expected value and swaps in a new value if they match), Fetch-and-Add (fetches the value and adds to it atomically).

Banker's algorithm in the answer keys: what should I know for the exam?

The keys compute Need = Max − Allocation, then scan P0, P1, P2 … repeatedly, continuing from where the last process was found (cyclic scan). Example (CAT-2 2024-25 B1): Available (3, 3, 2, 1) gives the safe sequence P0, P3, P4, P1, P2, and P1's request (1, 1, 0, 0) is granted because the state stays safe. Other valid sequences are accepted (the 2025-26 C1 key notes P0, P2, P1, P3, P4 as also correct). In 2025-26 C2, P2's request (0, 3, 0, 0) is refused because it exceeds P2's need (1, 0, 1, 2): always check Request ≤ Need first, then Request ≤ Available, then safety.

**The rule.** SRTF is the **preemptive** version of SJF. The CPU always runs the arrived process with the **shortest remaining time**.

**When to decide.** Look again whenever (1) a process **finishes**, or (2) a new process **arrives**. On an arrival, compare the newcomer's burst with the running process's **remaining** time. Preempt only if the newcomer is **strictly shorter**; on a tie the running process continues.

**Keep a "remaining" column.** Each time a process runs, reduce its remaining time. Decisions use remaining time, not the original burst.

**Waiting time with pieces.** A process may run in several pieces. Use **WT = CT − AT − BT**; it counts every period spent waiting. Response time (wait before the first run) is usually smaller.

Summarise When to run detection, and recovery for me

How often to invoke detection depends on how often deadlock is likely and how many processes would need rolling back (one for each disjoint cycle). If it is invoked at arbitrary times there may be many cycles and it is impossible to tell which thread caused the deadlock. Recovery by process termination: abort all deadlocked processes, or abort one at a time until the cycle is gone, choosing by priority, how long it has computed and how long it still needs, resources used and needed, how many processes must be terminated, and whether it is interactive or batch. Recovery by resource preemption: select a victim (minimum cost), roll it back to a safe state and restart it, and avoid starvation (the same process always picked as victim) by counting rollbacks in the cost.

Explain Shortest Remaining Time First

A **doctor's clinic** where the doctor always treats whoever needs the least time left. If a patient walks in needing 2 minutes while the current one still needs 7, the doctor pauses and sees the quick case first.

**The rule.** SRTF is the **preemptive** version of SJF. The CPU always runs the arrived process with the **shortest remaining time**.

**When to decide.** Look again whenever (1) a process **finishes**, or (2) a new process **arrives**. On an arrival, compare the newcomer's burst with the running process's **remaining** time. Preempt only if the newcomer is **strictly shorter**; on a tie the running process continues.

**Keep a "remaining" column.** Each time a process runs, reduce its remaining time. Decisions use remaining time, not the original burst.

**Waiting time with pieces.** A process may run in several pieces. Use **WT = CT − AT − BT**; it counts every period spent waiting. Response time (wait before the first run) is usually smaller.

Does an unsafe state mean deadlock?

No. Unsafe means the system cannot guarantee that every process finishes; deadlock may happen if processes ask for their maximum. A safe state guarantees no deadlock. Avoidance (the Banker's algorithm) simply never lets the system enter an unsafe state.

Can you teach me Semaphores from scratch?

**Mall parking with a display board.** The board shows free spaces (S). A car entering takes one (wait: S−1). If the board goes to −2, two cars are queued at the gate. A car leaving frees one (signal: S+1) and the first queued car drives in.

**What a semaphore is.** An integer S that can only be changed by two atomic operations:
- **wait(S)** (also P or down): S = S − 1. If S becomes **negative**, the calling process **blocks** and joins S's waiting queue.
- **signal(S)** (also V or up): S = S + 1. If S is still **≤ 0**, one waiting process (the first in the queue) is **woken up**.

**Reading the value.** In this (blocking) implementation, S = −k means **k processes are waiting**. A quick check: final S = initial S − (number of waits) + (number of signals).

**Two definitions you will meet.** Your Module 4 notes define the operations with **busy waiting**:
`P(S) { while (S <= 0) ; S--; }` and `V(S) { S++; }`. There a process that cannot enter keeps looping (spinning),
and **S never goes below 0**. OSTEP and the Theory "Semaphore" slides use the **blocking** version above, where S can go
negative. Both block the same processes at the same moments; only the number shown differs (busy-waiting value = the
blocking value, but never below 0). In an exam, say which definition you are using. The tutor accepts either.

**Uses**
- **Mutex** (binary semaphore, initial 1): `wait(mutex); critical section; signal(mutex);`
- **Counting** (initial n): controls access to n identical resources.
- **Producer–consumer:** mutex = 1, empty = n, full = 0. Producer: wait(empty), wait(mutex), add, signal(mutex), signal(full). Consumer: wait(full), wait(mutex), remove, signal(mutex), signal(empty).

**Classic bug.** If the producer does wait(mutex) **before** wait(empty) and the buffer is full, it sleeps while holding mutex, and the consumer can never get in: **deadlock**.

What's the difference between a mutex and a binary semaphore?

Both allow one process at a time and can start at 1. A mutex lock has an owner: only the process that locked it should unlock it. A binary semaphore has no owner: any process can signal it, which also makes it useful for ordering (e.g. a parent waiting for a child with a semaphore starting at 0).

Can you teach me Round Robin from scratch?

**Cricket nets practice.** Each batter gets 6 balls (the time quantum), then goes to the back of the line, even if they wanted more. A batter who gets out on ball 3 leaves early and the next one starts at once.

**The rule.** Keep a FIFO **ready queue**. Take the process at the **front** and run it for at most one **time quantum** q.
- If it finishes within q, it leaves, and the next process starts immediately (no idle remainder).
- If not, the timer interrupts it and it goes to the **back** of the queue.

**Queue order convention (important).** If a process arrives at exactly the moment another one's quantum ends, this course puts the **new arrival in the queue first**, then the preempted process. Always track the queue on paper: write it down after every slice.

**Choosing q.** A huge q makes RR behave like FCFS. A tiny q causes too many context switches. RR usually has worse average turnaround than SJF but much better **response time**, so it suits interactive systems.

What do our notes say about Deadlock prevention?

Prevention eliminates at least one necessary condition. (1) Eliminate hold and wait: allocate all resources a process needs before it starts; this lowers device utilisation. (2) Allow resource preemption: take resources from a process when a higher-priority process needs them. (3) Impose resource ordering: number every resource type and allow requests only in increasing order (R1 < R2 < R3), so no cycle can form. (4) Disallow mutual exclusion where possible by making resources sharable.

Banker's safety algorithm: what should I know for the exam?

1. Work = Available; Finish[i] = false for every i. 2. Find an i with Finish[i] = false and Need_i ≤ Work; if none exists go to step 4. 3. Work = Work + Allocation_i; Finish[i] = true; go to step 2. 4. If Finish[i] is true for all i, the system is in a safe state. Slide 231 version with flags: inputs are any 2 of the 3 matrices (Max, Need, Allocation) and any 1 of (Available, total number of instances). Step 1: flag[i] = 0 for all i; Need = Max − Allocation. Step 2: find Pi with flag[i] = 0 and Need_i ≤ Available. Step 3: if found, flag[i] = 1 and Available = Available + Allocation_i, go to step 2; else go to step 4. Step 4: if every flag is 1 the system is safe, otherwise unsafe. Total instances = Allocated + Available. In each step: compare Need with Available, then Available = Available + Allocated.

I don't understand first come first serve

**In a real computer.** A shared printer prints jobs in the order they were sent, and simple batch queues run jobs first-come-first-served.

**The rule.** Run processes in the order they **arrive**. FCFS is **non-preemptive**: a process keeps the CPU until its burst is finished. If two processes arrive at the same time, the one listed first goes first.

**How to solve an FCFS problem**
1. Sort the processes by arrival time.
2. Each process starts at the later of: its arrival time, or the moment the previous one finished.
3. If the CPU finishes before the next process arrives, the CPU is **idle** until it arrives.
4. Then CT, TAT = CT − AT, WT = TAT − BT.

**The convoy effect.** If a long process arrives first, every short process behind it waits for the whole long burst. Explain IPC in UNIX

Unix/Linux IPC mechanisms: pipes and FIFOs (an anonymous pipe(fd) gives one-way data flow between related processes such as parent and child: write(fd[1], …) to the write end, read(fd[0], …) from the read end; a FIFO is a named pipe in the file system usable by unrelated processes); message queues (discrete messages kept by the kernel, asynchronous); shared memory (a common segment mapped into several address spaces; fastest because there is no kernel copying, but needs semaphores; mmap() maps files or shared-memory objects); semaphores (integer synchronization primitives); signals (lightweight asynchronous event notifications such as SIGINT interrupt, SIGTERM termination request, SIGKILL forced termination, SIGCHLD child status change; not for bulk data); sockets (bidirectional, local Unix-domain or network). The IPC.pdf lab example: a server creates a shared-memory segment with shmget(key 5678, size 27, IPC_CREAT | 0666), attaches it with shmat(), writes the letters a–y and waits until the first byte becomes '*'; the client attaches with the same key, prints the data and writes '*'.

I don't understand Semaphores

**In a real computer.** A server with 10 database connections uses a counting semaphore set to 10: the 11th request waits until one connection is returned.

**What a semaphore is.** An integer S that can only be changed by two atomic operations:
- **wait(S)** (also P or down): S = S − 1. If S becomes **negative**, the calling process **blocks** and joins S's waiting queue.
- **signal(S)** (also V or up): S = S + 1. If S is still **≤ 0**, one waiting process (the first in the queue) is **woken up**.

**Reading the value.** In this (blocking) implementation, S = −k means **k processes are waiting**. A quick check: final S = initial S − (number of waits) + (number of signals).

**Two definitions you will meet.** Your Module 4 notes define the operations with **busy waiting**:
`P(S) { while (S <= 0) ; S--; }` and `V(S) { S++; }`. There a process that cannot enter keeps looping (spinning),
and **S never goes below 0**. OSTEP and the Theory "Semaphore" slides use the **blocking** version above, where S can go
negative. Both block the same processes at the same moments; only the number shown differs (busy-waiting value = the
blocking value, but never below 0). In an exam, say which definition you are using. The tutor accepts either.

**Uses**
- **Mutex** (binary semaphore, initial 1): `wait(mutex); critical section; signal(mutex);`
- **Counting** (initial n): controls access to n identical resources.
- **Producer–consumer:** mutex = 1, empty = n, full = 0. Producer: wait(empty), wait(mutex), add, signal(mutex), signal(full). Consumer: wait(full), wait(mutex), remove, signal(mutex), signal(empty).

**Classic bug.** If the producer does wait(mutex) **before** wait(empty) and the buffer is full, it sleeps while holding mutex, and the consumer can never get in: **deadlock**.

Quick check: In producer–consumer, the producer calls wait(mutex) and then wait(empty) when the buffer is full. What can happen?

What do our notes say about Multiprocessor locking, lock-free coordination and OS examples?

On multicore systems many threads may compete for the same lock (lock contention); only one wins and the rest spin or wait. Repeated atomic updates of the same lock cause cache-coherence traffic (cache-line bouncing): a lock can be correct yet slow. Scalable locks reduce contention: the ticket lock (take a token at a counter), queue-based locks where threads wait in a queue, the MCS lock (each waiting thread spins on its own queue node) and the CLH lock (a thread waits on its predecessor's state). Lock-free coordination uses atomic operations such as CAS instead of lock ownership, avoiding blocking, contention and deadlock in multi-lock designs. Examples: Solaris uses adaptive mutexes (spin if the holder is running on another CPU, otherwise sleep), condition variables, readers–writers locks for longer sections, and turnstiles with priority inheritance. Windows XP masks interrupts on uniprocessors, uses spinlocks on multiprocessors (a spinlocking thread is never preempted) and dispatcher objects (mutexes, semaphores, events like condition variables, timers) in signalled or non-signalled state. Linux before 2.6 disabled interrupts for short critical sections; 2.6 and later is fully preemptive and provides semaphores, spinlocks and reader–writer versions of both (on a single CPU spinlocks become enabling/disabling kernel preemption).

What do our notes say about Test-and-Set and Compare-and-Swap?

test_and_set(boolean *target) { boolean rv = *target; *target = true; return rv; } runs atomically: "tell me the old lock value and set the lock to busy". Lock usage with boolean lock = false: do { while (test_and_set(&lock)); /* critical section */ lock = false; /* remainder */ } while (true). P0 calls test_and_set, gets false, enters, and lock is now true; P1 calls it repeatedly and keeps getting true (busy waiting / spinning); when P0 sets lock = false, P1's next call returns false and it enters. Properties: mutual exclusion and progress yes, but bounded waiting is not guaranteed: with several competitors there is no queue, so a process can keep losing the race and starve. compare_and_swap(int *value, int expected, int new_value) { int old = *value; if (*value == expected) *value = new_value; return old; } runs atomically: "change the value only if it is still what I expect". Lock: while (compare_and_swap(&lock, 0, 1) != 0); /* critical section */ lock = 0;. P0 gets 0 back and sets lock to 1; P1 gets 1 back, lock unchanged, and retries until P0 sets lock = 0.

What is Banker's algorithm?

**Bank loans.** The bank has ₹10 lakh. Each business declares its maximum loan. The bank lends only if it can still see an order in which every business could get its full limit, finish its project and repay.

**The data.** For n processes and m resource types:
- **Available**: free instances of each resource.
- **Max**: the most each process may ever request.
- **Allocation**: what each process holds now.
- **Need = Max − Allocation**: what each process may still request.

**Safety algorithm**
1. Work = Available; mark every process unfinished.
2. Find an unfinished process with **Need ≤ Work** (every resource).
3. Pretend it finishes: **Work = Work + its Allocation** (it returns what it held). Mark it finished.
4. Repeat. If every process finishes, the state is **safe** and the order is a **safe sequence**. If you get stuck, it is **unsafe**.

**Many right answers.** A safe state usually has several safe sequences. Any order works as long as each chosen process has Need ≤ Work at its turn.

**Requests.** If a request > Need: error. If request > Available: wait. Otherwise pretend to grant it and run the safety algorithm; grant only if the result is safe. **Unsafe ≠ deadlock**: it means deadlock is *possible*.

Summarise CPU scheduling and the CPU–I/O burst cycle for me

CPU scheduling is the basis of a multiprogrammed OS: by switching the CPU among processes the OS makes the computer more productive. The objective of multiprogramming is to have some process running all the time, to maximise CPU utilisation. A process runs until it must wait, typically for an I/O request to complete; several processes are kept in memory (ready queue, waiting queue), and when one has to wait the OS takes the CPU away and gives it to another. Process execution is a cycle of CPU execution and I/O wait: processes alternate between a CPU burst and an I/O burst, ending with a final CPU burst.

Explain What a deadlock is

Deadlock is a state in which two or more processes are stuck forever because each is waiting for a resource held by another. Example: P1 holds R1 and needs R2 while P2 holds R2 and needs R1: who moves first? No one. It happens only when four conditions exist together: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption and circular wait. Deadlocks are handled by prevention, avoidance (Banker's algorithm) or detection and recovery. System model: resource types R1 … Rm (CPU cycles, memory space, I/O devices), each with Wi instances. A process uses a resource in the order request → use → release. Deadlock arises when processes hold some resources while waiting for others. Everyday and system examples of deadlock: printer and scanner (P1 holds the printer and waits for the scanner, P2 the opposite); database transactions locking rows A and B in opposite order; two mutex locks taken in opposite order by two threads; two programs locking files A and B in opposite order; four cars in a traffic intersection each waiting for the next; dining philosophers each holding one fork.

What are the three requirements of a critical section solution?

1. Mutual exclusion: at most one process is in the critical section.
2. Progress: if nobody is inside, the choice of who enters next can't be postponed forever, and only processes that want to enter take part.
3. Bounded waiting: a process that has asked to enter can be overtaken only a limited number of times.

What do our notes say about How the notes compute CPU utilisation, throughput and context switches?

Every worked example ends with the same performance summary. Total system time is measured from 0 to the last completion time (e.g. 25 ms in the FCFS-with-I/O example even though the first process arrives at 2). CPU utilisation = total CPU burst time / total system time × 100 (e.g. 21/25 = 84%). Throughput = number of processes / total system time (e.g. 5/25 = 0.2 processes/ms). Number of context switches = how many times the Gantt chart changes from one process to a different process; an idle gap is not counted when the same process resumes (P5 → idle → P5 is no switch) and the first dispatch is not counted. Without preemption FCFS gives N − 1 switches for N single-burst processes.

What is Round Robin?

**Cricket nets practice.** Each batter gets 6 balls (the time quantum), then goes to the back of the line, even if they wanted more. A batter who gets out on ball 3 leaves early and the next one starts at once.

**The rule.** Keep a FIFO **ready queue**. Take the process at the **front** and run it for at most one **time quantum** q.
- If it finishes within q, it leaves, and the next process starts immediately (no idle remainder).
- If not, the timer interrupts it and it goes to the **back** of the queue.

**Queue order convention (important).** If a process arrives at exactly the moment another one's quantum ends, this course puts the **new arrival in the queue first**, then the preempted process. Always track the queue on paper: write it down after every slice.

**Choosing q.** A huge q makes RR behave like FCFS. A tiny q causes too many context switches. RR usually has worse average turnaround than SJF but much better **response time**, so it suits interactive systems.

Explain Scheduling criteria and formulas

CPU utilisation = CPU busy time / total time × 100 (maximise). Throughput = number of completed processes / total time (maximise). Turnaround time TAT = completion time − arrival time (minimise). Waiting time WT = time spent waiting in the ready queue = TAT − CPU burst time (minimise). Response time RT = time of first CPU allocation − arrival time (minimise). Context switches: the number of times the CPU switches between processes; pure overhead (minimise). Fairness: each process gets an equitable share (maximise). The notes also state: TAT = waiting time + CPU burst time + I/O burst time (or TAT = WT + CPU burst when there is no I/O). In non-preemptive scheduling response time = waiting time, because a process starts only once. In preemptive scheduling response time ≤ waiting time.

What do our notes say about Theory slides: concurrency bugs and threads?

Concurrency bugs are non-deterministic and depend on the execution order. Non-deadlock bugs: atomicity bugs (an atomicity assumption is violated, e.g. one thread reads and prints a shared item while another modifies it; fix with locks, even for reads) and order-violation bugs (thread 1 assumes thread 2 has already run; fix with condition variables or semaphores). Deadlock bugs are covered in the deadlock notes. Threads: a thread is like another copy of a process that executes independently but shares the same address space (code, heap); each thread has its own program counter and its own stack. Processes created with fork share no memory and need IPC; threads share globals, so communication is easier and the memory footprint smaller. Concurrency = running several threads at the same time even on one core by interleaving; parallelism = running them on different cores at once. The OS schedules kernel threads independently, saving their context in a thread control block (TCB); every PCB has one or more TCBs; Linux pthreads are kernel threads. Two threads each incrementing a shared counter 10^7 times without a lock often end below 2 × 10^7, because counter = counter + 1 is several machine instructions: a race condition on a critical section, fixed by mutual exclusion (locks).

Summarise Process states and the PCB for me

States: new (being created), ready (waiting to be assigned to a processor), running (instructions are being executed), waiting (waiting for some event such as I/O completion), terminated (finished). The OSTEP-style slides name them running, ready, blocked (waiting for an event, e.g. a disk read; unblocked by the disk interrupt), new and dead. The Process Control Block (PCB, also called task control block) holds each process's information: process state, program counter, CPU registers, CPU-scheduling information (priority, queue pointers), memory-management information, accounting information (CPU used, elapsed time, limits) and I/O status (devices allocated, open files). The OS keeps a list of all active PCBs.

What do our notes say about Theory slides: semaphores in the blocking style?

These slides define a semaphore as a variable with an underlying counter and two functions: up/post increments the counter; down/wait decrements it and blocks the calling thread if the resulting value is negative. A semaphore with initial value 1 is a simple lock (binary semaphore = mutex). Semaphores can also order threads, like condition variables: e.g. a parent waiting for its child uses a semaphore initialised to 0. Producer/consumer needs two semaphores for signalling (one tracking empty slots so the producer waits when there are none, one tracking full slots so the consumer waits when there are none) and one semaphore as a mutex for the buffer. Incorrect solution: if the mutex is acquired before waiting on the empty/full semaphore, a waiting thread sleeps holding the mutex and the signalling thread can never wake it: deadlock.

Multilevel feedback queue scheduling – MLFQ: what should I know for the exam?

MLFQ is like MLQ but processes can move between queues based on their CPU usage or I/O behaviour; priorities change dynamically. CPU-heavy processes move down; I/O-bound or short processes stay up (and can move up). Each queue has its own time slice; higher queues have shorter slices; a process that uses its whole slice may be demoted. Preemption is allowed: a higher-priority queue interrupts a lower one. Classic setup: Q0 RR with quantum 8 ms, Q1 RR with quantum 16 ms, Q2 FCFS. A new process enters Q0 and gets 8 ms; if it does not finish it moves to Q1 and gets 16 more ms; if it still does not finish it is preempted and moved to Q2. If a process completes, or gives up the CPU for I/O, within its 8 ms its priority does not change and when it comes back to the ready queue it starts again in Q0. Question: a CPU-bound process needs 40 s; the quantum is 2 s at the first level and increases by 5 s per level (2, 7, 12, 17, 22).

Test-and-Set and Compare-and-Swap: what should I know for the exam?

test_and_set(boolean *target) { boolean rv = *target; *target = true; return rv; } runs atomically: "tell me the old lock value and set the lock to busy". Lock usage with boolean lock = false: do { while (test_and_set(&lock)); /* critical section */ lock = false; /* remainder */ } while (true). P0 calls test_and_set, gets false, enters, and lock is now true; P1 calls it repeatedly and keeps getting true (busy waiting / spinning); when P0 sets lock = false, P1's next call returns false and it enters. Properties: mutual exclusion and progress yes, but bounded waiting is not guaranteed: with several competitors there is no queue, so a process can keep losing the race and starve. compare_and_swap(int *value, int expected, int new_value) { int old = *value; if (*value == expected) *value = new_value; return old; } runs atomically: "change the value only if it is still what I expect". Lock: while (compare_and_swap(&lock, 0, 1) != 0); /* critical section */ lock = 0;. P0 gets 0 back and sets lock to 1; P1 gets 1 back, lock unchanged, and retries until P0 sets lock = 0.

Explain The critical-section problem

The critical section is the part of a program that accesses shared data or resources and must be protected. With n processes, each has a critical-section segment; when one process is in its critical section no other may be in its own. Each process asks permission in an entry section, then runs the critical section, an exit section and the remainder section. A correct solution must satisfy: 1. Mutual exclusion: only one process executes in the critical section at a time. 2. Progress: if nobody is inside and some processes want to enter, the choice of who enters next cannot be postponed forever (and only processes that want to enter take part). 3. Bounded waiting: there is a bound on how many times other processes may enter after a process has asked and before it is allowed in, so it is not overtaken forever. Kinds of solutions: software-based (Peterson's solution for two processes; the Bakery algorithm for N > 2 processes); hardware-based (synchronization hardware: atomic instructions). Semaphores and monitors are operating-system-level synchronization primitives; locks are often implemented at application level.

What do our notes say about Banker's algorithm data structures?

For multiple instances of each resource type. Each process must claim its maximum use in advance; a requesting process may have to wait; a process that gets all its resources must return them in finite time. The algorithm has two parts: the safety algorithm and the resource-request algorithm. With n processes and m resource types: Available (vector of length m; Available[j] = k means k instances of Rj are free), Max (n × m; Max[i,j] = k means Pi may request at most k instances of Rj), Allocation (n × m; currently allocated), Need (n × m; Need[i,j] = Max[i,j] − Allocation[i,j], what Pi may still request).

Explain Deadlocks in concurrent programs

Deadlock bug, classic form: Thread 1 holds lock L1 and waits for L2 while Thread 2 holds L2 and waits for L1. It occurs only if the executions overlap and a context switch happens after a thread has acquired just one lock. It appears as a cycle in the dependency graph, and all four conditions (mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait) must hold. Preventing circular wait: acquire locks in a fixed total (or partial) order, e.g. both threads take L1 before L2, or order locks by the address of the lock variable. Preventing hold-and-wait: acquire all locks at once, e.g. by first taking a master lock (reduces concurrency). Avoidance: if the OS knew which locks each process needs it could schedule them so deadlock cannot occur (the Banker's algorithm is popular but assumes knowledge rarely available in real life). Detect and recover: reboot or kill deadlocked processes.

What do our notes say about Deadlock avoidance and safe state?

Avoidance needs a priori information: each process declares the maximum number of instances of each resource type it may need. The avoidance algorithm examines the resource-allocation state (available, allocated, maximum demands) so that a circular wait can never happen. A system is in a safe state if there is a sequence <P1, P2, …, Pn> of all processes such that each Pi's remaining needs can be satisfied by the currently available resources plus the resources held by all Pj with j < i: if Pi's needs are not immediately available it waits until the earlier ones finish, then gets its resources, runs, releases them, and so on. Safe state → no deadlock; unsafe state → possibility of deadlock; avoidance ensures the system never enters an unsafe state. For a single instance of each resource type the resource-allocation-graph algorithm is used; for multiple instances, the Banker's algorithm. In the RAG scheme a claim edge Pi → Rj (dashed) says Pi may request Rj; it becomes a request edge when the request is made and an assignment edge when granted, and back to a claim edge when released.

Summarise Interrupt disabling and locks for me

Solution 1, interrupt disable: a process disables all hardware interrupts before entering its critical section and enables them on exit, so nothing else can run meanwhile. Not suitable for multiprocessors: disabling interrupts on one CPU does not stop the others. Solution 2, locks: a lock lets only one process access a shared resource at a time; a process must acquire the lock first, and if another process holds it the requester is blocked until it is released. Software-based locks use flags, turn variables or tickets: Peterson's algorithm (two processes), Dekker's algorithm (more complex, two processes) and the Bakery algorithm (more than two processes, token based). Hardware-based locks use atomic instructions.

Summarise Readers–writers problem for me

A database is shared by readers (only read) and writers (read and write). Several readers may read at the same time without harm, but a writer needs exclusive access: a writer together with any other reader or writer may cause inconsistency. Solution with two semaphores and a counter: readcount = 0 (number of active readers), mutex = 1 (protects readcount), wrt = 1 (shared by readers and writers; gives writers exclusive access). Writer: do { wait(wrt); /* perform the write */ signal(wrt); } while (true). Reader: do { wait(mutex); readcount++; if (readcount == 1) wait(wrt); signal(mutex); /* read */ wait(mutex); readcount--; if (readcount == 0) signal(wrt); signal(mutex); } while (true). The first reader locks writers out and the last reader lets them in; other readers can enter while a reader is inside. Theory notes version: case 1, two writers, a single semaphore wrmutex = 1 around each write. Case 2, one writer and one reader: semaphores wrmutex = 1 and mutex = 1 and a counter readers = 0, with the same reader protocol as above.

shortest job first in simple words please

**In a real computer.** Batch systems that know job lengths (e.g. scheduled reports on a server) run short jobs first so most users get results quickly.

**The rule.** Whenever the CPU becomes free, choose the process with the **shortest burst time among those that have already arrived**. SJF here is **non-preemptive**: once a process starts, it finishes. Ties are broken by arrival order.

**Two traps**
- A process that has **not arrived yet** cannot be chosen, even if it is shorter.
- A short job that arrives while another is running does **not** interrupt it (that would be SRTF).

**Why it is useful.** When all processes are available together, SJF gives the **minimum average waiting time** of any non-preemptive order: putting a short job before a long one saves the short job more waiting than it costs the long one.

**Its weaknesses.** The OS does not know the next burst length in advance; it estimates it from past bursts (exponential averaging). Long jobs can **starve** if short jobs keep arriving.

When scheduling decisions happen; preemptive vs non-preemptive: what should I know for the exam?

CPU scheduling decisions may take place when a process (1) switches from running to waiting (e.g. an I/O request), (2) switches from running to ready (e.g. an interrupt), (3) switches from waiting to ready (e.g. I/O completes), (4) terminates. For 1 and 4 there is no choice: a new process must be selected. For 2 and 3 there is a choice. The scheduler runs whenever a process is created, terminates, requests I/O and blocks, an I/O completes, or a timer interrupt occurs (preemptive scheduling). How it works: processes waiting for the CPU sit in the ready queue; the scheduler picks one using an algorithm; the dispatcher assigns it to the CPU; the process then completes, requests I/O (moves to waiting), or is preempted back to the ready queue. Non-preemptive (cooperative) scheduling: decisions only in cases 1 and 4; the running process keeps the CPU until it finishes or blocks; simpler; suits batch systems; example FCFS. Preemptive scheduling: the CPU can be taken away from a running process; better responsiveness; suits interactive systems; example Round Robin.

Explain Semaphores

A **parking lot with a display board** showing free spaces. Each car entering takes one space (wait). If the board goes negative, that many cars are queued at the gate. Each car leaving frees a space (signal) and lets the first waiting car in.

**What a semaphore is.** An integer S that can only be changed by two atomic operations:
- **wait(S)** (also P or down): S = S − 1. If S becomes **negative**, the calling process **blocks** and joins S's waiting queue.
- **signal(S)** (also V or up): S = S + 1. If S is still **≤ 0**, one waiting process (the first in the queue) is **woken up**.

**Reading the value.** In this (blocking) implementation, S = −k means **k processes are waiting**. A quick check: final S = initial S − (number of waits) + (number of signals).

**Two definitions you will meet.** Your Module 4 notes define the operations with **busy waiting**:
`P(S) { while (S <= 0) ; S--; }` and `V(S) { S++; }`. There a process that cannot enter keeps looping (spinning),
and **S never goes below 0**. OSTEP and the Theory "Semaphore" slides use the **blocking** version above, where S can go
negative. Both block the same processes at the same moments; only the number shown differs (busy-waiting value = the
blocking value, but never below 0). In an exam, say which definition you are using. The tutor accepts either.

**Uses**
- **Mutex** (binary semaphore, initial 1): `wait(mutex); critical section; signal(mutex);`
- **Counting** (initial n): controls access to n identical resources.
- **Producer–consumer:** mutex = 1, empty = n, full = 0. Producer: wait(empty), wait(mutex), add, signal(mutex), signal(full). Consumer: wait(full), wait(mutex), remove, signal(mutex), signal(empty).

**Classic bug.** If the producer does wait(mutex) **before** wait(empty) and the buffer is full, it sleeps while holding mutex, and the consumer can never get in: **deadlock**.

Can you teach me deadlocks from scratch?

**Gridlock at a four-way junction.** Every car has entered the junction and waits for the car in front, which waits for the next, in a circle. Nobody can reverse (no preemption).

**Deadlock.** A set of processes where each one is waiting for a resource held by another process in the same set, so none can ever continue.

**The four necessary conditions** (all must hold at the same time):
1. **Mutual exclusion:** a resource can be used by only one process at a time.
2. **Hold and wait:** a process holds at least one resource while waiting for another.
3. **No preemption:** resources are released only voluntarily.
4. **Circular wait:** a cycle P1 → P2 → … → P1, each waiting for the next one's resource.

**Resource-allocation graph.** Draw request edges (process → resource) and assignment edges (resource → process). No cycle → no deadlock. With **one instance** of each resource, a cycle **means** deadlock. With several instances, a cycle means deadlock is **possible**.

**Handling deadlocks.** **Prevention:** break one condition (e.g. request resources in a fixed global order to stop circular wait). **Avoidance:** only grant requests that keep the system in a safe state (Banker's algorithm). **Detection and recovery:** let it happen, detect, then abort or preempt.

Explain First Come First Serve

A **railway ticket counter**: whoever reaches the line first is served first, and nobody can cut in.

**The rule.** Run processes in the order they **arrive**. FCFS is **non-preemptive**: a process keeps the CPU until its burst is finished. If two processes arrive at the same time, the one listed first goes first.

**How to solve an FCFS problem**
1. Sort the processes by arrival time.
2. Each process starts at the later of: its arrival time, or the moment the previous one finished.
3. If the CPU finishes before the next process arrives, the CPU is **idle** until it arrives.
4. Then CT, TAT = CT − AT, WT = TAT − BT.

**The convoy effect.** If a long process arrives first, every short process behind it waits for the whole long burst. Example: bursts 8, 2, 1 arriving at 0, 1, 2 give waiting times 0, 7 and 8 (average 5). If the short jobs could go first, the average would drop a lot. FCFS is simple and fair by arrival order, but its average waiting time can be poor.
Can you explain it another way?

Picture a **single-lane road**. A slow truck enters first; two bikes join behind it. Nobody can overtake, so the bikes crawl behind the truck even though they could finish in seconds. That traffic jam behind one slow vehicle is the convoy effect.

Explain Round Robin

Round Robin is designed for time-sharing systems: like FCFS but with preemption. A time quantum (time slice), generally 10–100 ms, is the maximum CPU time a process gets in one turn before it is preempted. The ready queue is a circular FIFO queue: new processes are added to the tail; the scheduler picks the first process, sets a timer to interrupt after one quantum and dispatches it. If the quantum is larger than every burst, RR behaves like FCFS (non-preemptive in effect); if the quantum is smaller than the bursts it causes many context switches, which overloads the OS. Flow: select a process; if its remaining burst < quantum it executes to completion; otherwise it executes for one quantum, and if not finished it goes back to the tail of the ready queue. Ready-queue order used in the worked examples: when a process arrives at the same moment a time slice ends, the newly arrived process is put in the queue before the preempted process (Example 2 and the RR-with-I/O example both do this).

Summarise The four necessary conditions for me

Deadlock can arise only if all four hold simultaneously. Mutual exclusion: only one process can use a resource at a time (non-sharable resources). Hold and wait: a process holds at least one resource while waiting to acquire others held by other processes. No preemption: a resource cannot be taken from a process; it is released only voluntarily. Circular wait: a set of processes wait for each other in a circle (P0 waits for P1, P1 for P2, …, Pn for P0).

Explain Shortest Remaining Time First

A **doctor's clinic** where the doctor always treats whoever needs the least time left. If a patient walks in needing 2 minutes while the current one still needs 7, the doctor pauses and sees the quick case first.

**The rule.** SRTF is the **preemptive** version of SJF. The CPU always runs the arrived process with the **shortest remaining time**.

**When to decide.** Look again whenever (1) a process **finishes**, or (2) a new process **arrives**. On an arrival, compare the newcomer's burst with the running process's **remaining** time. Preempt only if the newcomer is **strictly shorter**; on a tie the running process continues.

**Keep a "remaining" column.** Each time a process runs, reduce its remaining time. Decisions use remaining time, not the original burst.

**Waiting time with pieces.** A process may run in several pieces. Use **WT = CT − AT − BT**; it counts every period spent waiting. Response time (wait before the first run) is usually smaller.

The critical-section problem: what should I know for the exam?

The critical section is the part of a program that accesses shared data or resources and must be protected. With n processes, each has a critical-section segment; when one process is in its critical section no other may be in its own. Each process asks permission in an entry section, then runs the critical section, an exit section and the remainder section. A correct solution must satisfy: 1. Mutual exclusion: only one process executes in the critical section at a time. 2. Progress: if nobody is inside and some processes want to enter, the choice of who enters next cannot be postponed forever (and only processes that want to enter take part). 3. Bounded waiting: there is a bound on how many times other processes may enter after a process has asked and before it is allowed in, so it is not overtaken forever. Kinds of solutions: software-based (Peterson's solution for two processes; the Bakery algorithm for N > 2 processes); hardware-based (synchronization hardware: atomic instructions). Semaphores and monitors are operating-system-level synchronization primitives; locks are often implemented at application level.

Explain Deadlock avoidance and safe state

Avoidance needs a priori information: each process declares the maximum number of instances of each resource type it may need. The avoidance algorithm examines the resource-allocation state (available, allocated, maximum demands) so that a circular wait can never happen. A system is in a safe state if there is a sequence <P1, P2, …, Pn> of all processes such that each Pi's remaining needs can be satisfied by the currently available resources plus the resources held by all Pj with j < i: if Pi's needs are not immediately available it waits until the earlier ones finish, then gets its resources, runs, releases them, and so on. Safe state → no deadlock; unsafe state → possibility of deadlock; avoidance ensures the system never enters an unsafe state. For a single instance of each resource type the resource-allocation-graph algorithm is used; for multiple instances, the Banker's algorithm. In the RAG scheme a claim edge Pi → Rj (dashed) says Pi may request Rj; it becomes a request edge when the request is made and an assignment edge when granted, and back to a claim edge when released.

Theory slides: semaphores in the blocking style: what should I know for the exam?

These slides define a semaphore as a variable with an underlying counter and two functions: up/post increments the counter; down/wait decrements it and blocks the calling thread if the resulting value is negative. A semaphore with initial value 1 is a simple lock (binary semaphore = mutex). Semaphores can also order threads, like condition variables: e.g. a parent waiting for its child uses a semaphore initialised to 0. Producer/consumer needs two semaphores for signalling (one tracking empty slots so the producer waits when there are none, one tracking full slots so the consumer waits when there are none) and one semaphore as a mutex for the buffer. Incorrect solution: if the mutex is acquired before waiting on the empty/full semaphore, a waiting thread sleeps holding the mutex and the signalling thread can never wake it: deadlock.
