Can you teach me banker's algorithm from scratch?

**Bank loans.** The bank has ₹10 lakh. Each business declares its maximum loan. The bank lends only if it can still see an order in which every business could get its full limit, finish its project and repay.

**The data.** For n processes and m resource types:
- **Available**: free instances of each resource.
- **Max**: the most each process may ever request.
- **Allocation**: what each process holds now.
- **Need = Max − Allocation**: what each process may still request.

**Safety algorithm**
1. Work = Available; mark every process unfinished.
2. Find an unfinished process with **Need ≤ Work** (every resource).
3. Pretend it finishes: **Work = Work + its Allocation** (it returns what it held). Mark it finished.
4. Repeat. If every process finishes, the state is **safe** and the order is a **safe sequence**. If you get stuck, it is **unsafe**.

**Many right answers.** A safe state usually has several safe sequences. Any order works as long as each chosen process has Need ≤ Work at its turn.

**Requests.** If a request > Need: error. If request > Available: wait. Otherwise pretend to grant it and run the safety algorithm; grant only if the result is safe. **Unsafe ≠ deadlock**: it means deadlock is *possible*.

Explain How the OS runs a process and switches

The OS creates a process by allocating memory and building its memory image (code and data loaded from the executable, a stack and a heap), opening the standard files (stdin, stdout, stderr) and initialising the registers so the program counter points at the first instruction; then it gets out of the way and the process runs directly on the CPU. A process consists of a PID, its memory image, its CPU context (PC, registers, stack pointer) and its open file descriptors. The OS timeshares the CPU: the policy decides which process to run, the mechanism does the context switch. System calls use a trap instruction: the CPU moves to kernel mode, switches to the kernel stack, saves the user context, and jumps to the handler found in the Interrupt Descriptor Table (IDT, set up at boot). Traps also happen on program faults and device interrupts. return-from-trap restores the context and returns to user mode. Before returning, the OS may switch to another process: when the process exited or was terminated, made a blocking call, or has run too long.

Explain Bakery algorithm

Mutual exclusion for N > 2 processes, one of the most famous solutions. Idea: when a process wants the critical section it takes a ticket number; the smallest ticket enters first; if two processes get the same ticket, the lower process id goes first (lexicographic order on (ticket, id)). Analogy: customers at a bakery take tokens and the smallest token is served at the single counter (customer = process, token = number, counter = critical section). Four stages: take a ticket; wait for processes that are still choosing tickets; compare ticket numbers; enter, then release the ticket. Shared data: int number[n] (ticket of Pi; 0 means Pi is not interested) and boolean choosing[n] (true while Pi is choosing its ticket, so nobody compares against a half-chosen ticket). I don't understand Banker's algorithm

**Lending cricket kits.** A team that finishes returns ALL the kits it was holding, so your pile of spare kits grows after each team finishes.

**The data.** For n processes and m resource types:
- **Available**: free instances of each resource.
- **Max**: the most each process may ever request.
- **Allocation**: what each process holds now.
- **Need = Max − Allocation**: what each process may still request.

**Safety algorithm**
1. Work = Available; mark every process unfinished.
2. Find an unfinished process with **Need ≤ Work** (every resource).
3. Pretend it finishes: **Work = Work + its Allocation** (it returns what it held). Mark it finished.
4. Repeat. If every process finishes, the state is **safe** and the order is a **safe sequence**. If you get stuck, it is **unsafe**.

**Many right answers.** A safe state usually has several safe sequences. Any order works as long as each chosen process has Need ≤ Work at its turn.

**Requests.** If a request > Need: error. If request > Available: wait. Otherwise pretend to grant it and run the safety algorithm; grant only if the result is safe. **Unsafe ≠ deadlock**: it means deadlock is *possible*.

What do our notes say about Theory slides: locks, spinlocks and sleeping mutexes?

A lock protects a critical section: all threads share the lock, one succeeds and becomes the owner, the others cannot proceed until the owner releases it (pthreads provides such locks). Goals of a lock: mutual exclusion, fairness (no starvation) and low overhead. Disabling interrupts is not enough in general: it is privileged and can be misused, and it does not work on multiprocessors; it is used only inside the OS on single-processor systems. A lock built from a plain flag fails: a thread may be interrupted after its spin ends but before it sets the flag, so the race just moves into the lock code. Hardware atomic instructions fix this: test-and-set builds a spinlock (spin until acquired), and compare-and-swap can too. Alternative: a sleeping mutex, where a contending thread gives up the CPU (yield() moves it from running to ready) instead of spinning. Most user-space locks are sleeping mutexes; locks inside the OS are spinlocks, and while holding one the OS must disable interrupts on that core (an interrupt handler could ask for the same lock and spin forever) and must never block.

Summarise Theory slides: concurrency bugs and threads for me

Concurrency bugs are non-deterministic and depend on the execution order. Non-deadlock bugs: atomicity bugs (an atomicity assumption is violated, e.g. one thread reads and prints a shared item while another modifies it; fix with locks, even for reads) and order-violation bugs (thread 1 assumes thread 2 has already run; fix with condition variables or semaphores). Deadlock bugs are covered in the deadlock notes. Threads: a thread is like another copy of a process that executes independently but shares the same address space (code, heap); each thread has its own program counter and its own stack. Processes created with fork share no memory and need IPC; threads share globals, so communication is easier and the memory footprint smaller. Concurrency = running several threads at the same time even on one core by interleaving; parallelism = running them on different cores at once. The OS schedules kernel threads independently, saving their context in a thread control block (TCB); every PCB has one or more TCBs; Linux pthreads are kernel threads. Two threads each incrementing a shared counter 10^7 times without a lock often end below 2 × 10^7, because counter = counter + 1 is several machine instructions: a race condition on a critical section, fixed by mutual exclusion (locks).

What is shortest job first?

**Photocopy shop.** The shopkeeper finishes the current job, then takes the customer with the fewest pages among those already in the shop. A 1-page customer walking in mid-job must wait for that job to end.

**The rule.** Whenever the CPU becomes free, choose the process with the **shortest burst time among those that have already arrived**. SJF here is **non-preemptive**: once a process starts, it finishes. Ties are broken by arrival order.

**Two traps**
- A process that has **not arrived yet** cannot be chosen, even if it is shorter.
- A short job that arrives while another is running does **not** interrupt it (that would be SRTF).

**Why it is useful.** When all processes are available together, SJF gives the **minimum average waiting time** of any non-preemptive order: putting a short job before a long one saves the short job more waiting than it costs the long one.

**Its weaknesses.** The OS does not know the next burst length in advance; it estimates it from past bursts (exponential averaging). Long jobs can **starve** if short jobs keep arriving.

Semaphores as defined in the Module 4 notes: what should I know for the exam?

A semaphore is a synchronization primitive with an integer state, accessed (apart from initialization) only through two atomic operations, wait() and signal(), used to control access to shared resources and to coordinate processes. Proposed by Edsger Dijkstra. wait() is P (Dutch proberen, "to test"); signal() is V (verhogen, "to increment"). They give higher-level synchronization than spinning on test_and_set: a process that cannot enter blocks or sleeps, the CPU does other work, and the finishing process signals a waiter. Definition in these notes (busy-waiting form): P(Semaphore S) { while (S <= 0) ; /* no operation */ S--; /* enters critical section */ } and V(Semaphore S) { S++; /* leaves critical section */ }. In this definition the semaphore is a non-negative variable shared between threads: S = 1 means nobody is in the critical section, S = 0 means some process is using it, and a process that finds S <= 0 keeps looping until S becomes positive. All changes to the value inside wait() and signal() must be atomic.

Summarise Deadlock detection for me

Detection lets the system enter a deadlock and then finds it: for single-instance resources with a wait-for graph (look for a cycle), for multiple instances with a Banker's-style algorithm. Detection algorithm: 1. Work = Available; for each i, Finish[i] = false if Allocation_i ≠ 0, otherwise true. 2. Find i with Finish[i] = false and Request_i ≤ Work; if none, go to step 4. 3. Work = Work + Allocation_i; Finish[i] = true; go to step 2. 4. If Finish[i] = false for some i the system is deadlocked, and every such Pi is deadlocked. The algorithm needs O(m × n²) operations. Example: five processes P0–P4, three resource types A (7 instances), B (2), C (6). Allocation: P0 0 1 0, P1 2 0 0, P2 3 0 3, P3 2 1 1, P4 0 0 2. Request: P0 0 0 0, P1 2 0 2, P2 0 0 0, P3 1 0 0, P4 0 0 2. Available 0 0 0. Sequence <P0, P2, P3, P1, P4> gives Finish[i] = true for all i: no deadlock.

Explain Extra slides: multi-level feedback queue

MLFQ learns from the past to predict the future: it aims to optimise turnaround (run short jobs first) and minimise response time without knowing job lengths in advance. Rules: Rule 1: if Priority(A) > Priority(B), A runs. Rule 2: if Priority(A) = Priority(B), A and B run in Round Robin. Rule 3: a new job is placed at the highest priority. Rule 4a: if a job uses up an entire time slice its priority is reduced; Rule 4b: if it gives up the CPU before the slice ends it keeps its level (so MLFQ approximates SJF). Problems: starvation when there are many interactive jobs, gaming the scheduler (issue an I/O just before the slice ends), and jobs changing behaviour. Rule 5 (priority boost): after some period S move all jobs to the top queue. Better accounting replaces 4a/4b: once a job uses up its time allotment at a level, regardless of how many times it gave up the CPU, it moves down. Why does Peterson's solution not work on modern CPUs?

Can you teach me race conditions and the critical section from scratch?

**Booking the last train seat.** Two people on IRCTC click 'Book' for the last berth at the same moment. If both read "1 seat left" before either writes "0 left", both get confirmed: a race condition. The booking update must be a critical section.

**Race condition.** When several processes or threads access **shared data** at the same time, and the result depends on the exact order in which they run, you have a race condition.

**Why count++ is not safe.** In machine code it is three steps: **load** count into a register, **add** 1, **store** it back. If two threads interleave these steps, one update can be lost.

**Critical section.** The part of the code that touches shared data. A correct solution must guarantee:
1. **Mutual exclusion:** at most one process is in its critical section at a time.
2. **Progress:** if nobody is inside, a process that wants to enter cannot be blocked forever by processes that don't want to enter.
3. **Bounded waiting:** after a process asks to enter, there is a limit on how many times others can enter before it.

**Solutions.** Peterson's algorithm (two processes, using `flag[]` and `turn`), hardware atomic instructions (test_and_set, compare_and_swap), mutex locks and semaphores.

What do our notes say about The four necessary conditions?

Deadlock can arise only if all four hold simultaneously. Mutual exclusion: only one process can use a resource at a time (non-sharable resources). Hold and wait: a process holds at least one resource while waiting to acquire others held by other processes. No preemption: a resource cannot be taken from a process; it is released only voluntarily. Circular wait: a set of processes wait for each other in a circle (P0 waits for P1, P1 for P2, …, Pn for P0).

Explain Extra slides: proportional-share scheduling

A fair-share scheduler guarantees each job a percentage of CPU time instead of optimising turnaround or response time. Tickets represent a share: A with 75 tickets and B with 25 should get 75% and 25%. Lottery scheduling draws a random winning ticket each time slice (A holds 0–74, B 75–99) and runs its owner; the longer the jobs compete, the closer they get to the desired shares, but for short jobs unfairness can be large. Ticket currency (users allocate tickets in their own currency, converted to global value), ticket transfer (hand tickets to another process temporarily) and ticket inflation (a process raises or lowers its own tickets). Implementation: walk the job list adding tickets until the running sum exceeds the random winner. Stride scheduling is deterministic: stride = a large number / tickets (10,000/100 = 100 for A, 10,000/50 = 200 for B); always run the process with the lowest pass value and then add its stride to its pass. A new job entering with pass 0 would monopolise the CPU.

Explain first come first serve like I'm new to it

A **railway ticket counter**: whoever reaches the line first is served first, and nobody can cut in.

**The rule.** Run processes in the order they **arrive**. FCFS is **non-preemptive**: a process keeps the CPU until its burst is finished. If two processes arrive at the same time, the one listed first goes first.

**How to solve an FCFS problem**
1. Sort the processes by arrival time.
2. Each process starts at the later of: its arrival time, or the moment the previous one finished.
3. If the CPU finishes before the next process arrives, the CPU is **idle** until it arrives.
4. Then CT, TAT = CT − AT, WT = TAT − BT.

**The convoy effect.** If a long process arrives first, every short process behind it waits for the whole long burst. Example: bursts 8, 2, 1 arriving at 0, 1, 2 give waiting times 0, 7 and 8 (average 5). If the short jobs could go first, the average would drop a lot. FCFS is simple and fair by arrival order, but its average waiting time can be poor.

Explain Semaphores as defined in the Module 4 notes

A semaphore is a synchronization primitive with an integer state, accessed (apart from initialization) only through two atomic operations, wait() and signal(), used to control access to shared resources and to coordinate processes. Proposed by Edsger Dijkstra. wait() is P (Dutch proberen, "to test"); signal() is V (verhogen, "to increment"). They give higher-level synchronization than spinning on test_and_set: a process that cannot enter blocks or sleeps, the CPU does other work, and the finishing process signals a waiter. Definition in these notes (busy-waiting form): P(Semaphore S) { while (S <= 0) ; /* no operation */ S--; /* enters critical section */ } and V(Semaphore S) { S++; /* leaves critical section */ }. In this definition the semaphore is a non-negative variable shared between threads: S = 1 means nobody is in the critical section, S = 0 means some process is using it, and a process that finds S <= 0 keeps looping until S becomes positive. All changes to the value inside wait() and signal() must be atomic.

(Module 4 notes, slides 55–60)

What is Race conditions and the critical section?

**Booking the last train seat.** Two people on IRCTC click 'Book' for the last berth at the same moment. If both read "1 seat left" before either writes "0 left", both get confirmed: a race condition. The booking update must be a critical section.

**Race condition.** When several processes or threads access **shared data** at the same time, and the result depends on the exact order in which they run, you have a race condition.

**Why count++ is not safe.** In machine code it is three steps: **load** count into a register, **add** 1, **store** it back. If two threads interleave these steps, one update can be lost.

**Critical section.** The part of the code that touches shared data. A correct solution must guarantee:
1. **Mutual exclusion:** at most one process is in its critical section at a time.
2. **Progress:** if nobody is inside, a process that wants to enter cannot be blocked forever by processes that don't want to enter.
3. **Bounded waiting:** after a process asks to enter, there is a limit on how many times others can enter before it.

**Solutions.** Peterson's algorithm (two processes, using `flag[]` and `turn`), hardware atomic instructions (test_and_set, compare_and_swap), mutex locks and semaphores.

What is shortest remaining time first?

**Hospital casualty desk.** The doctor always treats whoever needs the least time left. A patient needing a 2-minute dressing walks in while the current patient needs 7 more minutes: the doctor pauses and does the dressing first. If the newcomer needs exactly as long as what is left, the doctor just continues.

**The rule.** SRTF is the **preemptive** version of SJF. The CPU always runs the arrived process with the **shortest remaining time**.

**When to decide.** Look again whenever (1) a process **finishes**, or (2) a new process **arrives**. On an arrival, compare the newcomer's burst with the running process's **remaining** time. Preempt only if the newcomer is **strictly shorter**; on a tie the running process continues.

**Keep a "remaining" column.** Each time a process runs, reduce its remaining time. Decisions use remaining time, not the original burst.

**Waiting time with pieces.** A process may run in several pieces. Use **WT = CT − AT − BT**; it counts every period spent waiting. Response time (wait before the first run) is usually smaller.

Summarise FCFS – First Come First Serve for me

The simplest algorithm: the process that requests the CPU first is allocated it first, implemented with a FIFO queue. New processes (their PCBs) are added at the tail; when the CPU is free it goes to the process at the head, which is removed from the queue. FCFS is non-preemptive. Its average waiting time is often high and it is not suitable for time-sharing systems (convoy effect: short processes wait behind a long one).

SRTF (preemptive SJF). Solve using preemptive SJF: P1 AT=0 BT=10, P2 AT=3 BT=6, P3 AT=7 BT=1, P4 AT=8 BT=3.

**Rule.** SRTF: at every arrival compare remaining times. The shortest remaining time runs, and a running process is preempted only if a newcomer is strictly shorter.

**Decisions**
- t = 0: CPU is free; P1 has the shortest remaining time among the ready processes (remaining 10).
- t = 3: P2 has a shorter remaining time (remaining 6) than running P1 (remaining 7), so P1 is preempted.
- t = 7: P3 has a shorter remaining time (remaining 1) than running P2 (remaining 2), so P2 is preempted.
- t = 8: CPU is free; P2 has the shortest remaining time among the ready processes (remaining 2).
- t = 10: CPU is free; P4 has the shortest remaining time among the ready processes (remaining 3).
- t = 13: CPU is free; P1 has the shortest remaining time among the ready processes (remaining 7).

**Gantt chart:** [0–3] P1 → [3–7] P2 → [7–8] P3 → [8–10] P2 → [10–13] P4 → [13–20] P1

Summarise Resource-allocation graph and wait-for graph for me

A resource-allocation graph (RAG) shows who holds what and who waits for what. Process nodes are circles (P1, P2, …); resource nodes are squares or rectangles, with the number of instances shown inside (dots or a count, e.g. R1 (2)). A request edge Pi → Rj means Pi has requested Rj and is waiting; an assignment edge Rj → Pi means an instance of Rj is held by Pi. If the graph has no cycle there is no deadlock. If it has a cycle: with one instance per resource type there is a deadlock; with several instances per type there is only a possibility of deadlock. The wait-for graph removes the resource nodes and draws only processes: an edge Pi → Pj means Pi waits for a resource held by Pj. It is most useful when each resource has a single instance: then a cycle in the wait-for graph means deadlock. With multiple instances a cycle is only a warning sign.
